10021-tenterhooks:
Ada Leverson's 1912 novel, the second book of The Little Ottleys, opens with a verbal invitation and a small domestic war. Edith has not been feeling well, which seems no reason for her to be the center of interest. So her husband Bruce, jealous of an invalid's privileges, starts an indisposition of his own.

From Carlsbad, Bruce hears news and receives Edith's solicitous letter about his rheumatism, and the comedy of married rivalry unfolds. Leverson writes with wit and a light, ironic touch. Readers get an elegant comedy of manners, where the sharpest battles are fought over sympathy, attention, and who is truly unwell.
11507-the-lure-of-san-francisco-a-romanc:
Elizabeth Gray Potter and Mabel Thayer Gray wrote this 1915 romance around old San Francisco landmarks. Audley B. Wells drew the pictures. The Mission, Portsmouth Square, and Lotta's Fountain each get a chapter.

Chinatown and the Presidio appear as well. The city's past is told through its streets and squares. A love story runs through the guide. Concepcion waits ten years in hope and despair. A later pair argue whether she would have been happy had Rezánov returned and taken her to Petrograd. The book pairs a walking tour with old California romance.
12109-the-house-that-jack-built-one-of-r:
R. Caldecott's picture book The House That Jack Built, published by Frederick Warne and Company in 1878, turns the old cumulative rhyme into a sequence of illustrations. The text begins, this is the house that Jack built, then adds the malt that lay in the house, and the rat that ate the malt.

Each new line adds a creature or object, with Caldecott's lively drawings giving the rhyme a visual joke at every turn. The picture book's success helped establish the modern illustrated children's book, in which pictures do not merely decorate words but carry part of the story. The cumulative form teaches memory through repetition and laughter.
12914-one-hundred-best-books-with-commen:
John Cowper Powys published One Hundred Best Books in 1916 with commentary and an essay on books and reading. The opening essay asks a charming, perturbing question: what should a person who has read nothing at all read first? It admits the solemn goblin of responsibility that haunts any list maker. Powys writes with gusto and oddity.

Later notes praise D'Annunzio's fierce, coloured rhetoric, from the Triumph of Death to a superb account of Venice and the Doge's Palace. Powys judges each book by feeling as much as by fame. The volume suits readers hunting for a personal, opinionated guide to classic reading.
13182-prefaces-and-prologues-to-famous-b:
Edited by Charles W. Eliot for the Harvard Classics, Prefaces and Prologues to Famous Books, published 1909 to 1910, gathers the front matter of great works. Contents run from Caxton's prologues to Troy, Aesop, Chaucer, Malory, and Virgil, to Calvin's dedication of the Institutes. Notes and illustrations frame each piece for general readers.

One passage, from Raleigh's history, notes that Assyrian kings left little but fame, while Hebrew story survived time's consuming disease from cradle to today. Another, on art, treats Italy as a great storehouse, whose works once stayed in place but now scatter wide. The volume is a compact history of how authors introduced their books, from print's dawn to modern times.
13435-on-the-choice-of-books:
Thomas Carlyle's address to Edinburgh University students, given April 2, 1866, anchors this volume, with a life of the author, a farewell letter, and notes on his bequest. Carlyle urges students to choose books that truly teach, and to treat reading as a serious duty rather than idle pastime.

The biographical pages follow a man of genius honoured in his lifetime, with a medal struck by friends and a statue praised by Ruskin. Carlyle also protests the opening of sealed letters in the post office, calling it close kin to picking pockets. The book mixes counsel on reading with a portrait of a stern, famous teacher of his age.
13650-nonsense-books:
Edward Lear's Nonsense Books of 1894 collect four volumes with all original illustrations: the first Book of Nonsense of 1846. Nonsense Songs and Stories of 1871, More Nonsense Pictures of 1872, and Laughable Lyrics of 1877. The publishers' notice traces that history for readers who want Lear whole.

Daddy Long-legs cannot sing again because his six long legs oppress his bosom with despair, and crabs would gladly come to hear him hum. An alphabet in verse follows, from ice so white and nice that nobody tasted it, to a jackdaw hopping in a principal street, to a kite flown above houses into the sky. Lear's nonsense books remain a treasury of rhyme, drawing, and gentle absurdity.
13776-one-day-a-sequel-to-three-weeks:
An anonymous author wrote One Day as a sequel to the scandalous romance Three Weeks. Published in 1912, it opens with a prince tearing open a royal letter. Courts have arranged his marriage to Princess Elodie of Austria, and the embossed crown mocks him. He scowls at a toy that costs so much and means so little.

The prince longs for life, love, and freedom beyond dynastic duty. He declares he will live when his time comes, whatever sin or sorrow follows. The novel follows his rebellion against arranged marriage and court control. Its tone is passionate and melodramatic, in the manner of its predecessor. Readers of Edwardian romance will recognise the style at once.
13997-real-folks:
Mrs. A. D. T. Whitney published Real Folks in 1893, a domestic novel of New England family life. Chapters move from this way and that, through Luclarion, story-rail, and news coming to Homesworth. Waking up, eavesdropping in Aspen Street, and Hazel's inspiration follow. Cockles and crambo, witch-work, and crumbs add homely detail.

Children feed pigeons crumbs under pantry blinds, wondering what kind of day it is in other houses. Whitney writes of neighbours, kin, morning glories, and horseshoes with warm realism. Her folks feel ordinary and true, not heroic. The novel suits readers of Victorian domestic fiction. It shows Whitney's gift for family character.
14273-invisible-links:
Selma Lagerlöf's Invisible Links, translated from Swedish by Pauline Bancroft Flach, gathers tales bound by unseen connections. Contents include the spirit of fasting and Petter Nord, the legend of the bird's nest, the king's grave, and the outlaws. The legend of Reor, Valdemar Atterdag, Mamsell Fredrika, a fisherman's wife, a mother's portrait, and Uncle Reuben Downie among climbing roses follow.

Guilt and fate link the stories. Jofrid, mourning a dead child, insists God alone decides and lays repentance aside, until a knock wakes her husband Tönne in the night. A divorced woman, drawn to a shoemaker as a pickerel is drawn to a boat, suffers want while her child goes in rags and her husband stays absent. Lagerlöf, author of Gösta Berling, writes with folk clarity and moral weight, showing how choices pull distant lives together across a Swedish countryside.
14497-addresses-by-the-right-reverend-ph:
Phillips Brooks, Bishop of Massachusetts, delivered the addresses collected in this 1895 Philadelphia volume, covering service, thought, action, business, liberty, faith, and Abraham Lincoln. Brooks was among America's best-known preachers.

The opening address urges a life of service from John's gospel, while later talks defend the Christian business man, true liberty, and honest doubt. Brooks honors the skeptic even as he argues for Christ. The addresses show a liberal, humane pulpit voice, earnest and literary, speaking to Boston congregations at the century's end. Brooks's Lincoln address remains the volume's best-known piece.
14520-mavericks:
William MacLeod Raine's 1911 western novel takes its title from unbranded cattle, and from the unbranded men who claim them. Phyllis, a ranch girl, and her brother anchor a story of rustling, branding, and frontier justice.

A nester is caught red-handed, a young man declares himself a rustler and thief, and shots from ambush, escapes, and a hold-up follow across the range. Raine, a prolific western writer, keeps the action moving and the romance warm. The novel is a sturdy example of the early western, where honor is tested at the branding iron and the gun.
15529-songs-from-books:
Rudyard Kipling collected this volume of songs from his books with Macmillan in London in 1914, first edition October 1913, reprinted twice that month and again in November 1913 and 1914. His preface says he gathered practically all the verses and chapter headings scattered through his books. In several cases he gave in full a song from which only a few lines had been used.

The opening poem is Cities and Thrones and Powers. It muses that cities stand in time's eye almost as long as flowers. Flowers daily die, yet cities rise again from spent earth as new buds put forth. A contents list maps each song to its book: Second Jungle Book, Rewards and Fairies, Puck of Pook's Hill, Plain Tales, and more. The volume lets readers enjoy Kipling's verse apart from his prose, in the order of his own collecting.
16003-the-black-baronet-or-the-chronicle:
William Carleton's novel of Irish gentry life turns on Sir Thomas Gourlay, called the Black Baronet, and his plans for his daughter Lucy. Sir Thomas presses ahead with a marriage match between Lucy and Lord Dunroe, son of Lord Cullamore of Red Hall. Cullamore, newly recovered from ill health, has little taste for the match and doubts it will bring Lucy happiness.

Letters, interviews, and family pressure carry the plot, as fathers bargain over a young woman's future. Carleton fills the book with Irish estates, servants, and social rank, and with the clash between parental will and a daughter's hopes. The novel gives a rich, old-fashioned picture of Ireland's landed world and its marriage market.
16558-from-the-ranks:
Captain Charles King opens this 1887 army novel with a strange night at an old fort. A sentry on Number Five fires about half past three, by order of the officer of the day, then flatly refuses to speak of it. By nine in the morning, no one holds the full facts, and the officer of the day is already investigating.

King, himself a U.S. Army captain, writes with inside knowledge of fort life, rank, and discipline. The mystery drives the plot, while barrack scenes and soldier talk fill the background. Readers of military fiction will find a taut, well-told puzzle from a writer who knew the service first hand.
17085-juliana-horatia-ewing-and-her-book:
Horatia K. F. Eden, sister of Juliana Horatia Ewing, pairs a memoir of the children's writer with a choice of her letters. The letters were not meant for print, and they speak to kin about home, health, music, and the making of books. Eden picks passages that touch most closely on Ewing's life and work, set in date order beside the memoir.

Readers meet a writer who could shape words for song yet played no tool, and who taught with zeal even when illness kept her from key days. The book gives a warm, close view of a Victorian author at work, and it helps fans of her tales see where the stories came from. It is a family record as much as a literary life.
17126-five-happy-weeks:
Margaret E. Sangster's 1875 tale for children starts with a sick mother told by her doctor to leave home for five weeks. Papa plans the stay with care: the house will shut, and Grandma and the children will wait at Aunt Maria's in Norfolk until the parents call for them on the way home. Edith, Mabel, and Johnnie face the parting with worry and pluck.

Five weeks of small trials, kind kin, and home lessons follow, all told in gentle, moral prose of its day. The book suits young readers who like family stories with a warm end. It also shows Victorian home life plain: doctors' orders, aunts as anchors, and children learning to bear a short, sad parting.
17172-the-ethics-of-george-eliot-s-works:
John Crombie Brown's essay on the ethics of George Eliot's works, in its 1884 fourth edition, grew from a paper too long for periodicals. A friend's praise during Brown's last illness pushed it into print, and Brown planned to add Middlemarch and Daniel Deronda. The last pages were dictated to his daughter five days before his death, when writing had failed him.

Brown reads Eliot as a moral teacher, tracing duty, sympathy, and growth through her novels. His prose is earnest and Victorian, fond of close reading over theory. Eliot readers will find a warm, early critical voice, and a moving record of a critic finishing his work at life's end.
17390-hearts-and-masks:
Harold MacGrath, author of The Puppet Crown and The Man on the Box, published this novel in New York in 1905, with pictures by Harrison Fisher. A frontispiece shows five people dressed for a costume ball, four seated and one standing, which sets the book's tone of society, disguise, and romance. MacGrath was a popular novelist of light, stylish fiction.

Readers get a turn-of-the-century romance of masked balls, mistaken identities, and love affairs among fashionable people. The story moves in MacGrath's easy, theatrical manner, with pictures to match its glamour. It suits readers of Edwardian popular romance who enjoy wit, costume, and intrigue.
18104-among-famous-books:
John Kelman wrote Among Famous Books, printed in 1912 by Hodder and Stoughton in London, New York, and Toronto. Kelman, a minister and critic, gives ten lectures on books that shaped modern thought.

Lectures run from the gods of Greece and Marius the Epicurean to the two Fausts, Celtic revivals, Bunyan, Pepys, Sartor Resartus, and Chesterton's point of view. Kelman opens by warning that the Greek-Hebrew split flatters neither side. He writes with a preacher's clarity and a reader's love. It is a fine, old guide to great books, best for readers who like criticism with warmth.
18360-the-farmer-s-boy-one-of-r-caldecot:
Randolph Caldecott's picture book turns a farm song into pictures for children. Frederick Warne published it in Great Britain as one of Caldecott's picture books. Each verse adds a new charge to the farmer's boy, and each new animal brings its own cry, so the song grows verse by verse.

The boy first keeps his master's horses, with a gee-wo here and a gee-wo there, and a pretty lass invited to the banks of the Aire. Lambs follow with baa-baa, and hens with chuck-chuck, each verse repeating the cries that came before. Children get a cumulative rhyme made for reading aloud and joining in, with Caldecott's pictures carrying the fun of farm work and farm noise.
18588-george-borrow-the-man-and-his-book:
Edward Thomas wrote this study of George Borrow, published by Chapman and Hall in London in 1912, with portraits and illustrations. Thomas, author of The Life of Richard Jefferies, drew on Knapp's life of Borrow and Watts-Dunton's prefaces, with help from Thomas Seccombe and R. A. J. Walling.

Chapters take up Borrow's autobiography, his own hero, and the books that made his name, from Bible Society travels to gypsy lore. The book also quotes Borrow's letters to the British and Foreign Bible Society, giving a portrait of a restless, learned wanderer whose life and books were hard to separate.
18758-by-berwen-banks:
Allen Raine's Welsh novel, published by Hutchinson of London in its hundred-and-eleventh thousand, opens in Caer Madoc, a sleepy town two miles from the sea. The story begins on the evening of the year's busiest fair, with the High Street littered and the shows gone.

In the stable of the Red Dragon, ostler Deio and farrier Roberts agree that Caradoc Wynne's horse Captain must rest, and Roberts will walk him gently to Abersethin. Later chapters name the house on the cliff, a storm, the arrival of Gwynne Ellis, a vicar's story, an old register, and a web of fate. The novel follows Welsh town life through love, secrets, and the pull of the coast.
18958-the-brother-clerks:
Writing as Xariffa, the author of this 1857 tale sets two young brothers down in New Orleans. They arrive by steamer on the Mississippi, with little money and high hopes, and seek clerk work in the busy port city. The city itself, with its wharves and crowds, frames their first steps.

The elder brother Arthur is bold and warm, while younger Gulian is frail, quiet, and deep in thought. Their bond is tested by pride, indulgent parents, love, and hard choices in business and home life. Readers get a mid-century city novel about brotherly love, youth, and the cost of growing up.
18984-the-starbucks:
Opie Read wrote this novel in 1902 about the Starbucks, a family in the American South. The tale moves through small-town life, church, and kin ties, with a young preacher at its centre who once ran wild and now seeks a steadier path. Dialect speech gives the scenes their local colour.

Jim, the preacher, wrestles with love for Mrs. Mayfield, with old Jasper's plain wisdom, and with doubts about books, war tales, and truth telling. Neighbours watch, judge, and forgive in turn. Readers get a warm, talk-filled Southern novel about faith, pride, and the slow change of a restless man.
19361-the-babes-in-the-wood-one-of-r-cal:
Randolph Caldecott's picture book retells the old ballad of the Babes in the Wood in verse, with his own pictures. A Norfolk gentleman and his wife die young and leave two small children in the care of kin. The kin, tempted by the children's inheritance, hire two men to do away with them in the wood.

One hired man relents, the other does not, and the pair quarrel over the children's lives. The tale is sad, as old ballads often are, but Caldecott's art softens it with charm. It remains a classic nursery version of a story English children have known for centuries.
19647-a-hero-and-some-other-folks:
William A. Quayle was an American Methodist bishop and a popular writer of his day. His 1900 book A Hero and Some Other Folks mixes verse, sketches, and moral reflection. It opens with a poem on a deed done for freedom. The poem pictures joy running through the earth when a slave feels his soul climb toward manhood.

Quayle wrote for general readers, in a warm and pulpit-ready voice. Pieces like these were meant to praise courage and stir conscience. The freedom poem shows his abolition-era inheritance and his faith in moral progress. Readers today meet a once-famous churchman whose name has faded. The book preserves his style of popular religious writing.
19708-cape-cod-folks:
Sarah P. McLean Greene wrote this novel of Cape Cod folks; its New York printing appeared in the early nineteen hundreds with pictures from the play. Wallencamp people, from Grandma Keeler getting Grandpa ready for Sunday school to Becky and the Cradlebow, fill chapters of missions, beaux, funerals, and festivities.

Singers going home strike up a hymn about windows open toward Jerusalem, while Emily vows to waltz down the lane to something livelier. Greene's book, drawn from her own Cape life, charms with dialect, humor, and affection for a seaside town.
19868-the-milkmaid-r-caldecott-s-picture:
Randolph Caldecott's picture books remade children's illustration in the 1870s and 1880s. The Milkmaid belongs to his celebrated series of toy books. Caldecott retells the old tale of the milkmaid and her pail. His drawings dance with movement, humor, and country detail. Edmund Evans printed them in color with great craft. Together they set the standard the Caldecott Medal still honors.

The milkmaid's daydream of riches from one pail of milk is proverbial. Caldecott gives that fable fresh legs and laughter. His line influenced every picture-book artist after him. This volume is a small piece of that revolution. Readers meet the art that taught picture books to move.
1994-adventures-among-books:
Andrew Lang gathers essays on books and writers he loved, from Robert Louis Stevenson and Oliver Wendell Holmes to Mrs. Radcliffe, Smollett, Hawthorne, and Saint Augustine. The pieces first appeared in magazines of his day. Lang knew most of these writers personally or through their books, and his essays mix memory with criticism.

Lang writes as a reader first, recalling authors, weighing novels, and defending the pleasures of story and poetry. The volume suits anyone who likes literary talk that is learned without being dry, and personal without losing judgment. His praise for storytellers over system-builders runs through the volume, and it explains his lasting appeal to readers.
20150-notes-on-my-books:
Joseph Conrad wrote Notes on My Books, short essays on how his novels came to be. Conrad looks back on tales of the sea and far ports. He writes of cruel, serene skies and merciless sun in the tropics. Under such light, fine detail fades and strong outlines rule the eye.

Each note tells what sparked a book, a place, or a man he met. Readers learn how a sailor became one of English prose's great stylists. The notes are brief, grave, and full of his dark humor. They suit anyone who wants Conrad's own map of his life's work.
21361-patience-wins-war-in-the-works:
A London family firm in Bermondsey buys a steel works in the North of England in George Manville Fenn's tale of war in the works. The boy hero, his father, and his three uncles bring London methods north: better ways of working steel and clever new equipment. The local workforce, backed by the trade unions, objects violently.

Outrages follow against the newcomers and against workers who come round to their side. The uncles complain that London men would have been more sensible. Slowly the family's conduct in crisis wins the town over, which is the patience of the title. Fenn tells an industrial fight as one of his adventure tales, with the factory as battlefield.
21540-high-noon-a-new-sequel-to-three-we:
High Noon, issued without an author's name in 1911, continues the tale of Paul and his queen from Three Weeks. An afternoon express thunders from Paris toward paradise as the tale opens. Among the gay summer seekers rides one English gentleman to whom the world is gray.

The foreword speaks to the thousands who lived through Paul's sunrise of love. Those readers mourned his queen and loved his small son with him. Now, it promises, comes the calm peace of his life's high noon. The sequel trades on the fame of Elinor Glyn's daring romance, and Paul's past shapes every page.
2186-captains-courageous-a-story-of-the-:
Rudyard Kipling's sea tale, in this telling, follows a spoiled rich boy who falls from a liner and is hauled aboard a fishing schooner off the Grand Banks. Aboard, he must learn to work, to obey, and to earn the respect of hard men who fish for cod in dangerous waters. The schooner's crew becomes his school.

Kipling fills the book with the language and labor of fishing: dories, lines, fog, and long watches. The boy's change from pampered passenger to useful hand is gradual and earned. Young readers and lovers of sea stories get a stirring adventure about work, manhood, and the sea's hard lessons.
21901-the-birthday-party-a-story-for-lit:
Flora Lee's July birthday is planned with love and limits in The Birthday Party. Oliver Optic's Riverdale story book was published at Boston in 1864. Flora is a good girl who gives her parents little trouble, trusting that they know what is best for her. Her parents have money and gladly pay for a good time. Yet they will not give her pies that would hurt her, or let her lie in bed till noon.

Oliver Optic, whose real name was William T. Adams, wrote shelf loads of improving tales for children. This little book teaches its moral gently: true indulgence guards a child even from her own wishes. Writing the party notes is pictured at the front. It is a small, warm relic of American Sunday reading.
2225-captains-courageous-a-story-of-the-:
Harvey Cheyne, a rich and unruly boy, is washed overboard from an ocean liner and rescued by a Gloucester fishing schooner. Rudyard Kipling builds Captains Courageous around his hard education on the Grand Banks, where cod fishing, fog, and discipline replace luxury and tantrums. Captain Disko Troop runs a tight ship, and Harvey must earn his place.

The novel teaches the sea as a trade: baiting trawls, handling dories, and reading weather. Harvey's friendship with the captain's son Dan gives the story its warmth. By the voyage's end the boy has grown steadier and kinder, and the book closes as a classic tale of work remaking character.
22308-golden-moments-bright-stories-for-:
Golden Moments gathers bright stories for young folks, as its title promises. No author is named in the catalog record. One scene shows girls at work with flowers on a warm day.

Marie shakes petals off her dress and talks fast and boldly. The wreaths, she tells Sophie, are already done. Her fix is to fasten a rose to the end of Fanny's pigtails. Then, she says, they would indeed be rose-red. Moments like that show the book's tone: gentle, playful, and close to child life. Young readers were offered short, cheerful tales rather than hard lessons.
22604-children-and-their-books:
James Hosmer Penniman wrote Children and Their Books, a 1921 study of what young readers should read and why it matters. Penniman, a scholar of literature, argues that schools fail children by neglecting the imagination. Imagination, he writes, is the mind's creative power, without which no Newton finds gravity and no Columbus sails.

The world of make-believe, he insists, delights small children through and through. Wise teaching builds on that delight. The book surveys stories fit for children and the harm done by cheap, careless reading matter. It reflects an era when librarians and teachers fought hard over children's shelves. Parents and educators today can still profit from its plea to take young reading seriously.
22606-the-booklover-and-his-books:
The Booklover and His Books is a volume of essays on books and reading, published in 1916. The catalog record names no author. It is a browser's book by design: the author offers it not so much for steady reading as for reading by chapters, dipping in where interest leads.

An index provides the clue to whatever the volume holds on any topic, for those who consult it in an orderly way. Essays of this kind treated binding, printing, collecting, and the pleasures of the shelf. The book belongs to a shelf of gentle, learned companions for readers of its day. It still suits anyone who enjoys thoughtful talk about books as physical and cultural things.
23495-the-story-of-the-greeks:
H. A. Guerber wrote this elementary history of Greece for young pupils, as a first text or as extra reading, in an eighteen ninety six American Book Company edition. A frontispiece of Theseus and the Minotaur sets the tone: history told through people, not through dry dates.

Guerber argues that children grasp anecdotes of persons long before they grasp history proper, so each chapter leans on stories of heroes, kings, and citizens in the childhood of civilisation. Gods, wars, laws, and arts enter through lives lived, from mythic founders to statesmen of Athens and Sparta. Teachers and young readers will find a clear, story rich path into Greek history, built to be enjoyed before it is studied in depth.
24415-proud-and-lazy-a-story-for-little-:
Oliver Optic, author of The Boat Club, All Aboard, and The Woodville Stories, wrote this Riverdale story for little folks. It was published by Hurst and Company in New York. Its first chapter introduces Tommy Woggs, a funny little boy, proud and lazy. He thinks himself a man and that other people live only to serve and obey him. No boys or girls like him, since he orders them round and thinks himself better.

Tommy's father is a doctor and a rich man, able to afford servants. He is not rich enough to spoil the child. Wealth cannot buy wisdom: not all the money in the world would teach even a simple sum, nor buy the love and respect of others. Tommy must study like poor children to be wise, and treat them well to win good will. Readers get a proud, lazy boy taught his lesson.
24537-history-of-the-confederate-powder-:
Colonel George W. Rains, late of the Confederate Army, delivered this address before the Confederate Survivors' Association at Newburgh on Memorial Day, 26 April 1882. He spoke with some hesitation, he said, because the subject had absorbed his own thought, time, and energies during the war.

Rains describes building and running the Confederate powder works, the mills that made the gunpowder Southern armies depended on. Histories of war, he notes, say little about the manufactories behind the fighting. His address fills that gap from firsthand knowledge, and it remains a key source for the industrial history of the Confederacy.
2486-queer-little-folks:
Harriet Beecher Stowe's Queer Little Folks gathers children's stories of animals and children, from a hen that hatched ducks to a nutcracker with a history. The tales mix humor, moral lessons, and Stowe's warmth, written for the young readers who loved her domestic fiction. The animals behave with just enough human sense to charm.

The collection shows Stowe beyond Uncle Tom's Cabin, as a storyteller for the nursery. Its period morals and its kindness still appeal. Families and collectors of children's books will enjoy it. Stowe wrote these tales for her own grandchildren and for young magazine readers.
2507-complete-poetical-works:
Bret Harte, born in Albany in 1839 and raised in the rough young California of the gold rush years, made his name writing about miners, gamblers, and frontier towns. A short life sketch opens this volume, tracing his path from printer and journalist to the writer who gave the Pacific coast a place in American letters.

The poems that follow range from comic dialect verse to tender ballads of camp life, lost luck, and homes far away. Harte writes in the voices of the people he knew, mixing humor with plain feeling. The book serves as a full record of his verse, and a vivid window on the California he helped turn into legend.
25427-careless-kate-a-story-for-little-f:
Oliver Optic tells of Kate Lamb, a little girl who will not mind her mother at once. Called from her garden marigolds, she answers without looking up and comes only when she is ready. Her carelessness grows into falsehood, and one night she lies awake haunted by thoughts of hungry, crying children. Sent to bed without supper for the first time, she feels the weight of her conduct.

Kate's father speaks words that linger in her ears, and at last she tells the whole story. The tale, published by Lee and Shepard in 1889, teaches obedience and truth through a child's remorse rather than a lecture. Its chapters move from garden disobedience to confession and forgiveness.
25444-dolly-and-i-a-story-for-little-fol:
Oliver Optic, the pen name of William T. Adams, tells a plain moral tale for children. Katy Green of Riverdale, ten years old, is a good girl spoiled by one fault: she envies others their good things. When her younger sister Nellie receives a finer doll, Katy's pleasure in her own gifts turns sour. Her mother talks to her until she cries, and tries to show her how ugly envy makes her.

Nellie, sorry to see her sister unhappy, even offers to trade dolls, but their mother will not allow it. Katy seems to improve, yet still resents that Nellie's doll is finer. The story follows her slow struggle against a feeling the narrator calls wicked. Published by Lee and Shepard in 1864, it opens the Riverdale story books.
25461-bo-peep-story-books:
Bo-Peep Story Books gathers six classic fairy tales for young readers, published by Leavitt and Allen in New York. Cinderella, edited by Madame de Chatelain, opens the book: a widower's sweet daughter is set to drudgery by a haughty stepmother and her two proud daughters. She scrubs stairs and polishes floors while her sisters sleep on featherbeds, yet bears her ill treatment meekly.

The other tales are The Princess Rosetta, Fair One and Golden Locks, Beauty and the Beast, Little Red Riding Hood, and The Sleeping Beauty. In the Red Riding Hood tale, kindness saves the girl: she helps a poor old water-cress woman, spares a wasp and a tom-tit, and the green huntsman shoots the wolf. A fairy then promises that no wild beast shall ever harm her.
26345-girl-scouts-in-the-adirondacks:
Lillian Elizabeth Roy's Girl Scouts in the Adirondacks, copyrighted in 1921 by George Sully and Company, follows the Dandelion Troop into the mountains. Captain Mrs. Vernon, called Verny, leads Juliet Lee, Ruth Bentley, and other Elmertown girls in two touring cars toward Old Forge. Chapters promise a Friday jinx, another day of troubles, and mountains at last.

Later come a visit to Grey Fox Camp, a story of creation, being lost on the trail, and Jake's interview with a skunk. Lessons in tracking, a canoe trip, first aid, and shooting the rapids test the troop. A grand surprise closes the book. Mid-book scenes show the girls digging a marsh hole for drinkable water, with Dick proving his scout craft. The tale praises pluck and teamwork.
26378-the-care-of-books:
John Willis Clark's Care of Books, issued by Cambridge University Press in 1901, traces libraries and their fittings from the earliest times to the end of the 1700s. Clark, registrary of the university and fellow of Trinity College, grew the essay from his Architectural History of Cambridge. A short paper by Dom Gasquet on medieval monastic libraries opened his eyes to the field.

Clark's Rede Lecture of June 1894 tried to rebuild the monastic library from its fittings, showing how desks, chains, and presses shaped monastic rules. Later pages treat cathedral libraries, including Rouen, whose chapter held books by 1120 and built a library in 1424 to 1428. The book serves readers who love libraries as places, not only as collections of texts.
26627-the-island-house-a-tale-for-the-yo:
F. M. Holmes published this tale for young folks with S. W. Partridge at London in 1898, among a series that also offered Roast Potatoes, Dick and His Donkey, and The Children of the Marshes. It opens on a summer evening after a heavy storm, when old Mansy, walking home with parcels and a bulgy umbrella, hears a low sullen roar in the quiet country. The house she left safe stands changed before her.

Flood water turns the house into an island, and children, nurse, and servants must signal, float, and improvise. A boy and old Mansy wait in a tub while girls at a window work with candle-light, string, and an arrow to reach them. Tied wrists, an unwelcome visitor, and a young navigator fill six short chapters of a cozy Victorian adventure.
27513-the-book-of-the-national-parks:
Robert Sterling Yard, chief of the educational division of the National Park Service in the Department of the Interior, wrote this book of the national parks. It was published by Charles Scribner's Sons in New York in 1919, with maps and illustrations. A painting of Zoroaster, deep in the Grand Canyon, fronts the volume.

Yard opens with an essay on the appreciation of scenery, then treats the parks in groups. Granite parks include Yosemite the incomparable, the heart of the Rockies, and McKinley, giant of giants. Volcanic parks include Lassen Peak, Mount Katmai, and Mount Rainier, icy octopus. The book teaches readers how to look at grand scenery, and why the parks matter.
28098-holiday-tales-christmas-in-the-adi:
W. H. H. Murray's Holiday Tales: Christmas in the Adirondacks, copyrighted in 1897, holds two long stories set in the New York woods. The first follows John Norton, an old trapper, as he keeps Christmas in his cabin. The second, John Norton's Vagabond, follows a wanderer who crosses his path.

Both tales mix winter travel, hunting, and cabin talk with a plain moral about kindness to strangers. Snow, deer, and mountain streams fill the scenes, and the trapper's rough speech gives the book its flavour. Readers who like old-fashioned Christmas stories will find it warm and unhurried.
28736-heart-talks:
C. W. Naylor wrote this 1922 volume of confidential talks on the Christian life, reprinted in 1982 by Faith Publishing House in Guthrie, Oklahoma. The book gathers short talks with plain titles. They include What It Means to Trust the Lord, The Blessing of Dissatisfaction, and Why I Believe the Old Book. Blighted Blossoms, Meeting the Lions, and Egg-Shell Christians are among the rest. Later talks treat patience, trouble, prayer, and the practical side of religion.

Naylor writes as a pastor speaking one to one, aiming to comfort, encourage, strengthen, and instruct. The talks are brief, homely, and direct, using everyday pictures like a redbird's message and home-made clouds. Readers interested in plain American devotional writing get a representative volume, warm in tone and meant to be read a talk at a time.
28847-max-and-maurice-a-juvenile-history:
Wilhelm Busch wrote Max and Maurice, a juvenile history in seven tricks, translated from the German by Charles T. Brooks and published by Little, Brown in 1902. The preface warns readers about two youths who leer at lessons and teachers, tease creatures, climb fences, and steal apples, pears, and quinces, instead of turning their minds to useful learning. Their mischief, the verse says, ends sad and dreary.

The first trick shows Widow Tibbets, who keeps poultry for eggs, roast hens, and feather beds, and becomes the boys' first victim. Busch tells the whole history in pictures and verses, matching each prank to its punishment. Readers get a classic of mischievous children's verse, funny and stern at once, in the translation that made Busch known to American children.
29031-sir-william-herschel-his-life-and-:
Edward S. Holden of the United States Naval Observatory wrote this 1881 life and works of Sir William Herschel, published by Charles Scribner's Sons. Holden bases his account strictly on printed data: the memoir of Herschel's sister, Herschel's own writings, and memoirs and diaries of contemporaries. His review of Herschel's papers in the Philosophical Transactions and elsewhere aims to be of use to students.

Holden admits a fully satisfactory life must wait for the family papers in England, but argues that two generations after Herschel's death, no complete biography yet exists. His study presents the greatest of practical astronomers, and a profound philosopher, from scanty material. Readers get a careful, conscientious Victorian biography of the man who found Uranus and mapped the heavens.
30533-genera-and-subgenera-of-chipmunks:
John A. White writes Genera and Subgenera of Chipmunks, University of Kansas Publications, Museum of Natural History, volume five, number thirty-two, pages 543 to 561, with twelve figures, dated 1 December 1953. Editors include E. Raymond Hall, A. Byron Leonard, and Robert W. Wilson.

Contents move from introduction and history to methods, materials, and acknowledgments, then to evaluation of characters. White compares traits shared by Eutamias and Neotamias yet absent in Tamias, starting with structure of the malleus. The paper offers a technical revision of chipmunk classification, grounded in anatomy and museum specimens.
31017-ivory-apes-and-peacocks:
James Huneker wrote this 1915 book of criticism, published by Charles Scribner's Sons in New York, published in September 1915 and held here in a 1917 printing. It is dedicated to John Quinn, and its title comes from the verse in II Chronicles 9:21 about the ships of Tarshish bringing gold and silver, ivory and apes, and peacocks. Huneker's subjects are Joseph Conrad, Walt Whitman, Jules Laforgue, Dostoievsky and Tolstoy, Schoenberg, Wedekind, Moussorgsky, Cézanne, Vermeer, Matisse, Van Gogh, and Gauguin.

Chapters include The Genius of Joseph Conrad, A Visit to Walt Whitman, The Buffoon of the New Eternities on Laforgue, and Dostoievsky and Tolstoy and the younger choir of Russian writers. They continue with Arnold Schoenberg, Music of To-Day and To-Morrow, Frank Wedekind, and The Magic Vermeer. They end with Richard Strauss at Stuttgart and Max Liebermann and modern German art. It is a survey of poets, painters, composers, and dramatists.
31320-the-wooing-of-calvin-parks:
Laura E. Richards's 1908 novel, published by Dana Estes in Boston and illustrated, follows the wooing of Calvin Parks in eighteen chapters. It opens as Calvin checks his horse before a large, comfortable yellow house with a well-sweep, the house where Sam and Sim used to live. It introduces its principal characters, brotherly ways, Calvin's story, a candy route, and much concerning peppermints.

Later chapters bring board and lodging, match-making, playing s'pose, candy-making, John Alden with a difference, trade, Calvin's Waterloo, and merry Christmas. They go on to at last, contrast, toil and trouble, night, and morning, with characters including Mr. Cheeseman, Miss Hands, and Mary Sands. Warm, humorous, and New England to the core, the book is a gentle comedy of courtship and candy.
32401-the-girls-of-hillcrest-farm-or-the:
Amy Bell Marlowe's girls' novel, copyrighted in 1914, follows a group of girls who come to Hillcrest Farm after a chain of sudden changes. Early chapters bring Aunt Jane's proposal, a doctor's ruling, a pilgrimage, and the arrival of Lucas Pritchett. Neighbours, boarders, and a whisper in the dark soon fill the farmhouse with talk and trouble.

Later chapters add a runaway grandmother, a queer boarder, Widow Harrison's troubles, a temperance club, a hidden treasure, and a public sale. The secret of the rocks gives the story its mystery thread, while school, friendship, and household work carry its everyday warmth. Marlowe writes for young readers who enjoy farm life, lively neighbours, and a puzzle solved by steady girls.
3245-black-rock-a-tale-of-the-selkirks:
Ralph Connor sets this tale in the Selkirk Mountains, and an introduction vouches for its author. The introducer says he met Ralph Connor once on the Red River by canoe, once on the Assiniboine, and two or three times on the western prairies. That was not the name he gave, but it covers, the writer says, one of the most honest and genial fighters of the devil doing good work for men.

Black Rock itself is a mining camp in need of the gospel Connor's heroes carry. The novel mixes camp life, rough men, and a preacher's steady work. Readers who like Connor's frontier ministry tales will find the pattern here: a hard place, a faithful man, and a community slowly won to better ways.
3252-complete-project-gutenberg-oliver-w:
This omnibus gathers the whole Project Gutenberg works of Oliver Wendell Holmes Sr in one volume. The Autocrat of the Breakfast Table leads, with the Professor and the Poet at the same table following. Over the Teacups, Elsie Venner, and The Guardian Angel continue the set, with A Mortal Antipathy and pages from an old volume of life.

Bread and the newspaper, my hunt after the Captain, and the inevitable trial show Holmes the essayist and storyteller at large. Boston's beloved physician-wit talks medicine, books, and human nature in one urbane voice. Holmes whole, in one volume: table talk beside novels beside memoirs, in a single urbane voice.
32521-keep-well-stories-for-little-folks:
May Farinholt-Jones's Keep-Well Stories for Little Folks, published in Philadelphia and London in 1916, teaches hygiene to children through stories and songs. Farinholt-Jones was professor of hygiene and sanitation and resident physician at Mississippi Normal College. Her book opens with the wonderful engine, two little plants, and the story of a fly, followed by swat the fly and the story of the rain barrel. Malaria, Jack Frost, and a story of tuberculosis follow.

Later contents include two little windows, merry sunshine, a wonderful stream, two mills, a child's calendar, and the toothbrush brigade. Mr. Fly and Mrs. Mosquito, a hygiene song, our little enemies, temperance, the white ship, and first aid to the injured and the Boy Scouts carry the lessons on. Pauline Wright's illustrations accompany a book that made health rules vivid for young readers.
3254-complete-project-gutenberg-john-gal:
This omnibus gathers John Galsworthy's Project Gutenberg works in one file. The Forsyte Saga leads in three volumes: The Man of Property, with Indian Summer of a Forsyte, then In Chancery, then Awakening and To Let. Other novels follow, from The Dark Flower and The Freelands to Beyond, Villa Rubein, and A Man of Devon.

A Knight, Salvation of a Forsyte, The Silence, Saint's Progress, and The Island Pharisees continue the set. The Country House, Fraternity, The Patrician, and The Burning Spear round out a long shelf. Together they trace Galsworthy's England: property, class, and conscience across a generation, in the steady, humane prose that won him the Nobel Prize.
33413-the-story-of-books:
Gertrude Burford Rawlings's Story of Books traces how books were made, kept, and spread, from classical times to early printing. Her chapters move from the preservation of literature and books in classical and medieval times to the beginning of printing. They take up who invented movable types, and Gutenberg and the Mentz press. Later chapters follow early printing in Italy, England, and Scotland.

The book belongs to a useful knowledge series, with a frontispiece of early printers at work, and it suits readers who love the history of reading itself. Rawlings writes plainly, with a scholar's care for detail. For book lovers, it is a delightful history of the object they hold, from scroll to press.
33682-old-coloured-books:
George Paston surveys old coloured books in this 1905 Methuen volume, with sixteen coloured plates. Chapters treat Rudolf Ackermann, Thomas Rowlandson, William Combe; the Cruikshank brothers, David Carey, Charles Molloy Westmacott, Pierce Egan and Theodore Lane, George Cruikshank; Henry Alken, and Charles James Apperley. Chapters also treat Robert Smith Surtees; and the Pickwick illustrators Robert Seymour, Robert William Buss, and Hablôt Knight Browne.

Plates show Dr. Syntax in the glass house, gamblers linked in folly's noose, the subscription room at Brooks's, Vauxhall Gardens, death's dance, and Tom and Jerry in the saloon at Covent Garden. Plates also show a racehorse, Jorrocks lecturing on hunting, and among others. Paston writes for collectors and lovers of illustrated books, tracing how hand-coloured aquatint and engraving shaped Regency and Victorian visual culture.
33995-where-the-path-breaks:
Captain Charles de Crespigny wrote this novel of a soul between worlds, published in Toronto in 1916 for Humphrey Milford. The story opens in dim twilight, where a spark of life glitters on a vast gray cliff above a dead gray sea. The spark wakes to warmth and to knowledge of its own life, then to a deeper knowledge: it was a man, and it is dead.

The soul, tired after a struggle almost forgotten, must dream back and know itself as it was before it wakes to what it is. Crespigny writes with patience and a sense of eternity. The novel offers a strange, moving tale of death, memory, and return.
3400-complete-project-gutenberg-william-:
This large file gathers a wide sweep of William Dean Howells in one place, assembled by Project Gutenberg contributors rather than issued as a single book by the author. Its three parts cover studies, novels, and plays, so a reader can move from his literary criticism to his fiction and then to his short stage farces without changing volumes. The contents list names works on Henry James, Emile Zola, and other writers alongside full novels.

Because it is a compilation, the file works best as a sampler and a reference shelf. A reader can test Howells on his own heroes, such as Cervantes, Dickens, and Thackeray, then turn to his stories of American middle class life. Anyone new to Howells will find the range of his career here, from sharp critical essays to domestic novels and light comic plays.
3432-quotations-from-the-project-gutenbe:
David Widger gathered this small file of quotations from the works of Mark Twain, the first in his series of quotation books for Project Gutenberg. It does not retell Twain's novels or essays. Instead it lifts short, sharp passages from across his writing and sets them side by side, so a reader can browse his wit without opening a long book.

Twain's humor, his distrust of fine talk, and his eye for human folly all appear in brief form. The file works as a sampler for new readers and as a handy source of lines for speakers and writers. Those who want full stories should turn to the novels themselves, but this set gives a quick taste of why Twain's sentences still get quoted.
3459-quotations-from-the-project-gutenbe:
David Widger gathered this file of quotations from John Galsworthy, the second in his series of quotation books for Project Gutenberg. It is not a novel or a play, but a set of short passages lifted from Galsworthy's writing and placed side by side. A reader can dip in anywhere and meet his voice in brief form.

Galsworthy, best known for The Forsyte Saga, wrote about property, class, and family duty with cool irony. These extracts show his eye for social manners and his sympathy for people trapped by custom. The file works as a sampler for new readers and as a source of short lines, while the full novels remain the place for his stories.
3471-quotations-from-the-project-gutenbe:
David Widger gathered this file of quotations from Charles Dudley Warner, the third in his series of quotation books for Project Gutenberg. Warner, a Hartford editor and essayist who co wrote The Gilded Age with Mark Twain, wrote about travel, gardens, and American manners. This file lifts short passages from his work and sets them together for browsing.

Readers meet Warner's easy, observant voice in brief form: remarks on books, on nature, and on the habits of his time. The set works as an introduction for those who have not read Warner and as a handy source of lines. His longer essays and travel books give the fuller context for the sentences quoted here.
4040-the-pedler-of-dust-sticks:
A children's storybook opens with the Pedler of Dust Sticks, a tale told to a visitor charmed by a portrait from Hamburg. Other pieces follow, on a grave, the mighty deeds of ABC, a child at her mother's grave, evening prayer, and a butterfly.

The stories are short, moral, and homely, written for young readers of an earlier age. They favor kindness, faith, and the small wonders of home over grand adventure. Parents reading aloud will find plain tales with clear lessons, in the manner of old illustrated gift books for children.
425-familiar-studies-of-men-and-books:
Robert Louis Stevenson studies nine figures of letters and life in this essay volume, drawn from magazines. Victor Hugo, Robert Burns, Walt Whitman, Henry David Thoreau, François Villon, Charles of Orleans, Samuel Pepys, John Knox, and Yoshida Torajiro each get a searching portrait. Stevenson owns that no one mind can master so many ages and lands.

His essays weigh craft, faith, and character with wit and candor. Burns stands as Scotland's national voice; Hugo as a bold innovator; Villon as poet and thief in one. The book shows Stevenson as critic at his best, frank, learned, and always personal in judgment.
455-the-university-of-hard-knocks:
Ralph Parlette turns his popular lecture into this plain-spoken book on learning from trouble. Delivered more than twenty-five hundred times to lyceum and Chautauqua crowds, the talk argues that hard knocks complete the schooling that books begin. Parlette keeps the lecture's spoken form, as if talking straight to the hall.

Chapters treat failure, pluck, and the daily tests that shape character. He quotes scripture and Shakespeare, but his voice stays homely and direct. The book reads as a cheerful sermon for strivers: take your knocks, learn their lesson, and keep going.
5133-quotations-from-john-l-motley-works:
This small volume gathers quotations from John Lothrop Motley's History of the Netherlands, selected by the Project Gutenberg editor David Widger. Motley's history, a classic of nineteenth-century American scholarship, tells the Dutch struggle against Spain for independence and religious freedom.

The quotations are arranged for readers who want Motley's most striking passages without reading the whole history at once, and the editor invites suggestions for favourite passages to add. The book works as a tasting menu for Motley's prose and as a quick reference for students of the Dutch revolt.
5348-ragged-dick-or-street-life-in-new-y:
Horatio Alger's Ragged Dick, or Street Life in New York, introduces Dick, a bootblack of the streets. Its chapters follow Johnny Nolan, Dick's new suit, Chatham Street and Broadway, a pocket-book, and Dick's early history. Later chapters bring a scene in a Third Avenue car, Dick as a detective, a room on Mott Street, and Micky Maguire.

Alger's most famous hero rises by honesty, pluck, and a tutor's help, in the rags-to-respectability pattern that made Alger a byword. The book offers young readers a lively portrait of old New York street life. It remains the classic statement of the Alger myth of self-help.
5831-the-riches-of-bunyan-selected-from-:
Jeremiah Chaplin selects devotional passages from John Bunyan in The Riches of Bunyan, prepared for the American Tract Society and published in New York in 1850. William Williams supplies an introductory notice, and contents open with God in glory, majesty, justice, and holiness, before moving through further themes of faith. The selections draw on Bunyan's wider works beyond his famous allegory.

Readers get Bunyan as a preacher and comforter, in short passages suited to daily reading and meditation. The book favors plain, earnest prose over argument, letting Scripture and experience speak together. It suits readers of Puritan devotion, Bunyan lovers, and anyone seeking a compact anthology of seventeenth-century spiritual writing.
7481-the-three-clerks:
Anthony Trollope, born in London in 1815, sets this novel among young men in government offices, the world he knew from his own civil service years. Three clerks, starting together in the lower ranks, face the temptations of Victorian London: ambition, debt, love, and the shortcuts that promise quick success. The introduction suggests the perfect place to read it: under a tree in Kensington Gardens on a summer day.

Trollope follows his clerks through offices, lodgings, and drawing rooms, with the humor and moral sharpness that made him famous. One climbs by talent and luck, another falls by fraud, and the third learns steadiness the hard way. The novel is a young man's guide to getting on, and a warning about what getting on can cost.
7871-dutch-fairy-tales-for-young-folks:
William Elliot Griffis's Dutch Fairy Tales for Young Folks opens with a mermaid flying from the sky bearing cheeses. An entangled mermaid, proud of her looks, dwells in a pool half salt and half fresh near the sea. Other tales bring a boy wanting more cheese and a princess with twenty petticoats.

A cat and cradle, Prince Spin Head, a boar with golden bristles, an ice king, elves, and kabouters and bells follow. A woman with 366 children and Santa Klaas with Black Pete close the set. Through Holland's canals and fields, Griffis gives young readers wonder, humor, and a taste of Dutch folk life.
818-the-aeroplane-speaks:
H. Barber, a captain in the Royal Flying Corps, wrote this guide to help the ordinary reader grasp the aeroplane and the pilot's life. He states two aims: to explain the machine and its joys and troubles, and to offer something of practical use. The book is his first effort as an author, written from flying experience.

Barber describes controls, engines, wind, and the feel of flight in plain terms, with the pilot's view to the fore. He writes for the curious layman, not the engineer, and his tone is eager and direct. The book is a lively record of early military flying, when the aeroplane was still a wonder and a risk.
8220-remarks:
Bill Nye, Edgar W. Nye, published Remarks with over one hundred and fifty illustrations by J. H. Smith, opening with verses by Bret Harte on Ah Sin. Nye's directions explain the book's plan: it is not designed for any one class, but is a universal repository of thought, containing some of his best thoughts. Though omitting any thought he judged better left unthought, which is why the book is not so large as intended. The humour that follows is deadpan, self-mocking, and American.

Nye was one of the most popular humorists of the Gilded Age, and Remarks shows why: short pieces, jokes, and observations on everyday life, delivered with a wink. The illustrations add to the fun. For readers of American humour, the volume is a classic of its kind, and a reminder of how the West laughed at itself.
855-clocks:
Jerome K. Jerome wrote this short piece on clocks, in the comic, reflective vein of his best essays. He muses on the tyranny of timepieces, on clocks that gain, lose, or stop, and on the human habit of watching the hands while life slips by. The transcriber's note keeps his old spellings, such as to-night and to-morrow.

Jerome's humour is gentle and domestic, turning a household object into a mirror of our fuss and folly. The piece is brief, but it shows his gift for finding philosophy in the everyday. It suits readers who like a light essay that makes them smile at their own watch, and then think twice about it.
8592-poetical-works:
George Gilfillan edited this volume of the poetical works of Charles Churchill, the eighteenth-century satirist, with a memoir, critical essay, and explanatory notes. Gilfillan opens by placing Churchill among writers who, in Goldsmith's phrase, narrowed great gifts to party ends: a man who might have been poet, hero, or saint. Became a fierce satirist, an unlucky politician, and a profligate who died young.

The poems themselves attack the politics, theatre, and society of Georgian London with speed and bite, naming names and sparing no one. Gilfillan's notes help modern readers follow jokes aimed at long-dead targets. The book suits readers of Augustan satire who want Churchill entire. A Victorian editor's sympathetic but frank life of a talent that burned fast and left a sharp mark.
8899-three-weeks:
Elinor Glyn introduces Three Weeks to American readers in 1907, answering misunderstanding and misrepresentation from nearly the entire English press and a section of the public. For her, the Lady of the novel was a deep study, the analysis of a strange Slav nature who, from circumstances, education. Her general view of life, stood beyond ordinary laws of morality. If she were studying a tiger, Glyn says, she would not give it a spaniel's attributes because the public might prefer a spaniel. She would portray it accurately, even so.

The novel itself follows an Englishman and an older, married Slav noblewoman through three weeks of passionate love in Switzerland and Venice, ending in tragedy. Glyn's frank treatment of female desire made the book notorious and bestselling. Readers today meet a key text of early twentieth-century popular romance.
941-just-folks:
Edgar A. Guest wrote these homely poems for just folks, dedicated to the little mother and the memory of the big father. The title poem speaks of queer folks who talk of weather and good times. Roses budding and bees on nectar sprees appear, with the scarlet fever scare and other small trials of family life woven in.

Guest's verse is plain, rhymed, and sentimental, praising home, work, and neighbourly kindness. He was the people's poet of his day, read aloud at kitchen tables across America. The book charms readers who like simple, heartfelt verse, where everyday life is treated as worthy of song.
9567-narrative-and-legendary-poems-compl:
Volume one of Whittier's works holds his complete Narrative and Legendary Poems, revised with his own notes. The book opens with The Vaudois Teacher, The Female Martyr, and The Funeral Tree of the Sokokis, then runs through Cassandra Southwick, The Bridal of Pennacook, and Barclay of Ury. Skipper Ireson's Ride, The Sycamores, and Telling the Bees follow. Each poem carries head-notes on its source and date.

Later poems in the volume span Among the Hills, Mabel Martin, and The Pennsylvania Pilgrim, with tales of faith, exile, and home. Whittier's voice stays plain and earnest throughout. A reader gets the full narrative Whittier in one volume, and the best start for his storytelling verse.
addresses-by-the-right-reverend-phillips: Phillips Brooks, bishop of Massachusetts, delivers these addresses, published at Philadelphia in 1895 by Henry Altemus. The contents run from The Beauty of a Life of Service and Thought and Action through The Duty of the Christian Business Man and True Liberty. The Christ in Whom Christians Believe and Abraham Lincoln close the volume. The opening address takes the words of Jesus from the eighth chapter of Saint John, that the truth shall make you free. It asks the purpose and result of that freedom.
adventures-among-books:
Andrew Lang ranges across his reading life in essays first printed in magazines, as his preface records, this text following the 1912 Longmans edition. Recollections of Robert Louis Stevenson stand near the front, written by a friend who shared Stevenson's tastes. Other chapters treat Oliver Wendell Holmes, William Morris's poems, and Mrs. Radcliffe's novels.

Lang writes on Smollett, Hawthorne, Saint Augustine's Confessions, the supernatural in fiction, and the art of storytelling itself. A final essay, The Paradise of Poets, looks at where poets rank the dead. The book is a scholar-poet's commonplace shelf, learned without heaviness, and it invites readers to wander their own libraries.
among-famous-books: John Kelman lectures among famous books, guiding readers through great works with a minister's warmth and a critic's eye. The lectures open on the pleasures and duties of reading, then turn to individual books and authors. Kelman's aim is not scholarship alone but friendship with books, and the habit of reading well.
b09-luther-good-works:
Martin Luther wrote A Treatise on Good Works in 1520 to answer a plain question: if faith alone saves, what should a Christian do? His answer walks through the Ten Commandments one by one. Each command becomes a guide to the shape of a faithful life at home, at work, and in prayer.

Luther teaches that a work is good because faith makes the worker right, not the other way around. The first command, trust in God, anchors all the rest. The treatise is his fullest work on daily morals from those years. It shows the Reformation speaking to kitchens and workshops, not only to scholars.
black-rock-a-tale-of-the-selkirks:
Black Rock, a novel by Ralph Connor, tells of a mining and lumber settlement in the Selkirk Mountains of western Canada. Connor knew that frontier world from his own missionary work there, and an introduction by George Adam Smith stresses that firsthand knowledge. A young minister, Mr. Craig, arrives among rough camps where drink and gambling do heavy damage.

Christmas Eve in a lumber camp opens the tale, followed by a saloon fight the men call their Waterloo. Mrs. Mavor's story deepens the human cost of camp life. Craig and his allies form a league against drink, hold a first communion, and watch their pact strain and break. Connor mixes adventure, humor, and open Christian appeal in a portrait of men fighting for cleaner lives.
britannica-1911-algae-occurrence-in-the-:
Occurrence in the Rocks, a section of the Algae article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica, asks why so few algae survive as fossils. Soft algal tissue rots away, so preservation is rare except where the body is hardened with silica, as in the diatoms, or with carbonate of lime, as in the coralline algae. The section calls the poor record unsurprising on that ground alone.

Yet descent makes the puzzle pointed, since mosses and vascular plants are believed to spring from algal ancestors, implying an age of algae before the Carboniferous forests. Many Silurian and Devonian remains once described as algae rest on evidence now judged inadequate. Calcareous Siphonales are well represented from the Silurian to the Tertiary, while diatoms appear only from the chalk onward. The Devonian fossil Nematophycus is believed to be a kelp-like alga. Fossil algae grow frequent only in late Secondary and Tertiary formations.
britannica-1911-barracks:
Barracks are the buildings that house military or naval forces. They hold quarters for officers, warrant officers, non-commissioned officers, and men. They also hold messes and recreation rooms, regimental offices, shops, stores, stables, and vehicle sheds. The word came through French from a late Latin term for a bar. It usually names permanent brick or stone buildings for troops in peacetime.

Hut barracks of corrugated iron lined with wood also count, built near training grounds with somewhat less room, closer to camp conditions. The 1911 Britannica entry, a very long one, works chiefly through the British system. Accommodation follows the Barrack Synopsis, an official schedule. It lays down, item by item, the buildings and fittings each unit is authorized to have. Its rules come from decisions made by authority over time.
captains-courageous-a-story-of-the-grand:
Rudyard Kipling sent a spoiled rich boy to sea school in Captains Courageous, his novel of the Grand Banks cod fleet. Harvey Cheyne, fifteen, son of a railroad millionaire, washes off a liner in the North Atlantic fog. A fishing schooner picks him up, and Captain Disko Troop refuses his money and puts him to work beside the captain's son Dan.

Harvey baits lines, cleans fish, stands watch, and learns the whole hard economy of the Banks through one season. Kipling fills the decks with dialect, weather, gear, and men's talk, drawn from real Gloucester fishermen. The boy who returns to his parents has been remade by wages and work. It remains the great boys' book of the fishing fleets.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-altar-candles:
An altar candlestick has five parts: foot, stem, knob at mid-stem, bowl catching wax drippings, and pricket, the sharp point holding the candle. A spring tube holding a small candle may replace the pricket. Early lights hung from ceilings or walls or stood on pedestals, fed with oil as canthari or holding candles as phari.

No evidence puts candlesticks on the altar before the tenth century, and Leo IV allowed only saints' relics and the Gospel book there. Acolytes carried candlesticks set on the sanctuary floor, as Eastern churches still do. By the thirteenth century Durandus describes a candlestick at each altar corner, and the custom became general in the sixteenth.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-arawaks:
The Arawaks, also called Aruacans, were the first American native peoples met by Columbus, not to be confused with the Aroacas, linguistically allied to the Chibchas of Colombia. Arawak-speaking tribes spread widely over South America, from the Paraguay sources to Lake Maracaibo's northwestern shores. They also spread from the eastern Andes slopes of Peru and Bolivia to the Atlantic coast of Guyana. Columbus met them in 1492 in the Bahamas, then in Haiti, Cuba, Jamaica, and Puerto Rico.

That century, and perhaps for centuries before, Arawak peoples held the Greater Antilles, and may once have held every West Indian island. Then Caribs, pressing from the Venezuelan mainland, gradually took the southern Antilles and drove Arawaks northward, who feared their aggressors. The entry maps a language family across a continent and an island world remade by invasion.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-candlesticks:
Little is known of the earliest candlesticks in Christian churches. Constantine's gifts to the Lateran and Saint Peter's seem mostly stands and hanging chandeliers for lamps. They include two sets of seven bronze candelabra ten feet high before the altars, though those may not have held wax tapers. Great hanging crowns of gold and silver, bearing fifty, eighty, or 120 little dolphin branches each holding lamps, lit the great feasts.

Rohault de Fleury counts 8,730 lights that Constantine destined for the Lateran basilica, and such crowns lasted through the Middle Ages across East and West. Besides these, plain candlesticks were surely in use from very early times, and the seven candlesticks of the Apocalypse likely mirror a feature already familiar in worship. Smaller survivors, like a bronze chandelier shaped as a basilica holding a dozen lights, show how these works were built.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-censorship-of:
Censorship of books is the supervision of the press to prevent abuse of it. Every lawful authority charged with shielding its subjects from a pernicious press has the right to exercise it. Censorship falls into two kinds, ecclesiastical and civil, depending on whether a spiritual or secular authority practices it. It works in two ways: before printing or publication, by examining a work, and after printing or publication, by repressing or prohibiting it.

The classical word censura covers both meanings, especially in Roman Church legislation. In later civil law it came to mean almost only examination beforehand. Wherever past centuries speak of abolishing censorship, only the prior kind is meant. Freedom of the press, the reverse of censorship, is nowhere unlimited. Abuse may be condemned and punished under common law, and old censorship has nearly everywhere given way to stricter press laws.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-chinooks:
An entry on the Chinooks, an Indian people of the lower Columbia River from the Dalles to its mouth. Divided into Lower and Upper Chinooks, they lived in large wooden houses holding several families, grouped into villages on the north bank of the Columbia and Willamette, each under an independent chief. Their staple food was salmon with roots and berries, and they were great traders, carrying goods in high-prowed canoes as far as Nootka Sound.

Contact with whites brought a trade jargon of Chinook and Nootkan words, later widened by other tongues, and it brought ruin as well. The entry presents the tribe as an example of civilisation unprepared by religion, thinned by vice and disease until the Lower Chinooks died out. Missionary visits by Father Demers in 1840 baptised children but won few lasting converts, and today no more than 300 Chinooks remain, mostly on reservations in Oregon.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-creeks:
An ethnological entry describes the Creeks, an important confederacy of Indian tribes and remnants, chiefly of Muskogian stock. They once held most of Georgia and Alabama's central and southern lands, but now live in eastern Oklahoma. Their name first belonged to their homeland, the Creek Country, not to the people.

The dominant tribe is the Maskoki, about half the whole body, alongside Hichitee, Koasati, and Yuchi, each with its own language. The Seminole began as a separated band of Creeks. In the colonial period the Creeks held the balance between English Carolina and Spanish and French Florida and Louisiana. Their English alliance helped destroy the Franciscan missions of upper Florida in 1702 to 1708, carrying off 1,400 mission Indians as slaves.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-index-of-proh:
Once the Church's official list of books Catholics were forbidden to read, the Index is explained here as part of a larger code of book law. The list itself was the second and larger half of a volume called the Index librorum prohibitorum, which gathered all church legislation about books. A separate article on book censorship covers the wider system behind it.

Books reached the list by decree of a Roman congregation, such as the Holy Office or the Congregation of the Index, with papal approval in common form. The pope could also act alone by bull or brief. The entry explains that process. Complaints led to a book being examined. A listing then shaped what Catholic readers could read.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-italo-greeks:
Greeks in Italy who keep the Byzantine rite are the Italo-Greeks of this entry, sorted into three classes. First, church communities that have followed the Greek rite since Byzantine days; second, Greek colonies in port cities and at Rome. Third, descendants of Greeks and Albanians who fled the Turkish conquest of the Balkans in mass migration to southern Italy, founding towns and strong local groups.

That third group long kept its own tongue and customs and still keeps the Greek rite, though in other ways it has merged into Italian life. Whether any southern Italian or Sicilian diocese used the Greek rite before the eighth century is hard to say. Gradual hellenization and many Greek monasteries surely shaped liturgical life. The entry maps a rite surviving across conquest, migration, and absorption.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-liturgical-bo:
Liturgical books are the official volumes that hold the texts and rubrics, the directions, for a church's public worship. They are the yardstick for what counts as liturgical: a rite is official only if it stands in one of these books, a point the entry stresses against private devotion books.

Early Christians had no such volumes beyond the Bible, since forms lived in memory and habit. This long survey traces how fixed prayers came to be written down, then gathered into the Missal, Breviary, and kin. Roman books come first, followed by shorter accounts of the books of other rites, East and West.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-prayer-books:
By prayer books, usage means a store of prayer forms meant for private devotion, set apart from service books, which hold the set forms of public worship. The early Christian centuries left no such book, and we cannot be sure any then stood. Bishop Serapion's Prayer book, is more a Pontifical than a prayer book, and was surely not meant for private use.

Later prayer books swelled with high claims. A prayer said ere a picture of Christ crucified bore, by a supposed grant of Gregory III, as many days of indulgence as wounds in the Saviour's Body. A supposed grant of Boniface VIII speaks of eighty thousand years. In truth no curb on print stood in the early sixteenth century. The Congregation of the Index came only after the Council of Trent, so ere Trent booksellers were free to print near any wild claim that might help sales.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-raskolniks:
Raskolniks, from the Russian raskol, schism or splitting, is a general name for dissidents from the Established Church in Russia. This encyclopedia entry groups under it the many offshoots of the Greek Orthodox Church of the Russian Empire, as Russian historians and church writers use the term. Strictly, the name covers only those who kept the outward forms of the Byzantine Rite. Others, who dropped its ritual as well as its teaching, fall under sectarianism instead.

The entry treats both kinds together, since either form of dissent is little known outside Russia. It compares the Raskolniks to an antithesis of Protestantism against Catholicism within Russian Orthodoxy. Later splits produced the Encyclicalists, who backed the tsar and agreed with the Established Church on main points, and the Controversialists, who denied those points. A third group, the Yedinovertsi or Uniates, entered union with the Established Church while keeping all their peculiar practices.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-silvester-jen:
Silvester Jenks, theologian born in Shropshire about 1656, died in December 1714. He was schooled at Douai College, where he taught philosophy from 1680 to 1686. He later preached in ordinary to James II. The Revolution of 1688 sent him fleeing to Flanders. Returning to England, he labored as a missionary in or near London and was named Archdeacon of Surrey and Kent by the chapter.

In 1711 Propaganda elected him Vicar Apostolic of the Northern District, but he died of paralysis before consecration. His works include A Contrite and Humble Heart of 1692 and Practical Discourses on the Morality of the Gospel of 1699. Later came The Whole Duty of a Christian of 1707 and A Short Review of the Book of Jansenius of 1710.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-franks:
Germanic tribes banded along the Rhine's right bank, from Mainz to the sea, form the confederation at the centre of this entry. Roman writers first name the Franks in a battle of about 241. In the third century some crossed into Belgic Gaul along the Meuse and Scheldt, and Rome, after failed efforts to expel them, settled for alliance.

Julian's victory in 359 did not destroy them, and the Franks of Belgium turned peaceful settlers, even backing Rome against the invasion of 406. Clovis, conversion, and the Merovingian kingdom carry the tale forward, with law, church life, and the slow making of France. It is a full account of a people who outlasted the empire they served.
clocks:
Jerome K Jerome opens Clocks by dividing the species in two: the clock that is always wrong and glories in it, and the clock that is right until you rely on it. From that distinction he spins a short comic essay on household timepieces, church clocks, and human self-deception. Appearance, he suggests, is a king who must be kept up at great effort.

Jerome treats clocks as characters with morals, praising honest wrongness over respectable fraud. The Lord-of-Lies passage in the middle shows his satire widening from mantelpieces to all mankind bowing before King Appearances. The piece is brief, genial, and exact, a good taste of the humor that made Jerome famous well beyond Three Men in a Boat.
complete-poetical-works:
Bret Harte's Complete Poetical Works gathers the verse of the Argonaut Edition, opening with a biographical sketch of the California writer. The sketch follows Harte from Albany to California in 1854, through jobs as miner, teacher, express messenger, and printer, to the editorship of the Overland Monthly. Poems are grouped as national pieces, Spanish idyls and legends, dialect verse, and miscellaneous poems.

Here are John Burns of Gettysburg, the mission legends of Padre Junípero, and Dickens in Camp. The dialect section holds Plain Language from Truthful James, the famous Heathen Chinee poem, with The Society upon the Stanislaus and other mining-camp ballads. Harte's poems made him famous beside his tales; this volume shows their full range, from Civil War sentiment to frontier comedy.
complete-project-gutenberg-john-galswort:
John Galsworthy's works are gathered in this collected volume, and the contents open with the Forsyte books in their order. The Man of Property stands as the first volume of the saga, followed by the interlude Indian Summer of a Forsyte and In Chancery; Awakening and To Let complete the third volume. The chronicle of the Forsyte family's property instinct is the spine of the set.

The other novels are shelved beside it: The Dark Flower, The Freelands, Beyond, Saint's Progress, The Island Pharisees, The Country House, Fraternity, and The Patrician. Villa Rubein and Other Stories and Five Short Tales hold the shorter fiction, including The Apple Tree and The First and Last. Essays and studies, from the Inn of Tranquility pieces to Quality, close the collection. It is a working library of Galsworthy between two covers.
complete-project-gutenberg-oliver-wendel:
Oliver Wendell Holmes's writings are gathered here in one collected volume, and the contents read as the map of a double career. The breakfast-table books come first: The Autocrat, The Professor, and The Poet at the Breakfast Table, with Over the Teacups to close the series. Those table-talk volumes made him famous on two continents.

The novels follow: Elsie Venner, The Guardian Angel, and A Mortal Antipathy. Pages from an Old Volume of Life gathers essays.
